difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion: the stimulus treats a necessary condition for success as if it were sufficient. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument with plausible structure, and two choices replicate superficially similar but structurally distinct errors. Students who misread the conditional direction will choose a trap.
stimulus: To be licensed as a clinical pharmacist in this state, a candidate must pass the national board examination. Dr. Reyes has passed the national board examination. Therefore, Dr. Reyes is licensed as a clinical pharmacist in this state.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only employees who have completed the mandatory safety training are permitted to operate heavy machinery. Yusuf has not completed the mandatory safety training. Therefore, Yusuf is not permitted to operate heavy machinery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To qualify for the regional science fair, a student must submit a written project proposal. Naledi submitted a written project proposal. Therefore, Naledi qualifies for the regional science fair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All award-winning documentaries address a social issue of broad public concern. This documentary addresses a social issue of broad public concern. Therefore, this documentary will win an award.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Engineers who graduate from accredited programs generally earn higher starting salaries. Marcus graduated from an accredited program. Therefore, Marcus probably earned a high starting salary.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No one who has been convicted of fraud can serve on the city council. Ingrid has not been convicted of fraud. Therefore, Ingrid is eligible to serve on the city council.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats 'pass the national board exam' as sufficient for licensure, when the argument establishes only that it is necessary (you must pass to be licensed). Choice B replicates the exact move: submitting a proposal is a stated requirement (necessary condition), and the argument treats satisfying that requirement as sufficient for qualification. Same necessary/sufficient confusion at the same conclusion strength.
explanations.A: This is valid reasoning. If only safety-trained employees may operate machinery, and Yusuf hasn't trained, then Yusuf correctly cannot operate it. No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Replicates the necessary/sufficient confusion: a stated requirement (necessary condition) is treated as sufficient to guarantee the outcome.
explanations.C: Close but structurally different. The premise here is a universal affirmative ('all award-winning documentaries have Y'), so arguing from Y to award-winning commits affirming-the-consequent. The stimulus's flaw derives from a necessary-condition statement ('must pass'), not a universal affirmative about a class. Although the logical form is related, the surface language and premise structure differ — it is a trap for students who conflate the two.
explanations.D: The premise uses 'generally,' making this a probabilistic/base-rate argument, not a necessary-condition argument. A different flaw family — off-by-dimension.
explanations.E: Invalid reasoning but a different flaw: the argument negates the antecedent (if convicted → ineligible; not convicted → eligible). The stimulus commits affirming the consequent of a necessary condition, not denying the antecedent.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole compositional fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from a property of its parts. Answer choices are drawn from varied domains with surface plausibility; one choice commits the inverse (whole-to-part) fallacy, one is valid, and one introduces a percentage/absolute-number confusion to serve as a trap.
stimulus: Each individual thread used in the weaving of this Moroccan carpet is extraordinarily fine and delicate. Therefore, the carpet itself must be extraordinarily fine and delicate.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every clause in this municipal ordinance was drafted by a specialist in administrative law. Therefore, the ordinance as a whole is a masterwork of administrative law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Brazilian rainforest ecosystem is extraordinarily complex. Therefore, each species that inhabits it has evolved a complex set of adaptive behaviors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each of the silicon chips in this processor is manufactured to nanometer tolerances. Therefore, this processor operates at nanometer tolerances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the tiles in this mosaic are a vivid shade of cobalt blue. Therefore, the mosaic as a whole probably appears predominantly cobalt blue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every musician in the orchestra rehearsed individually for over one hundred hours. Therefore, the orchestra as a whole rehearsed for a very large number of hours.

explanations.correct: The stimulus argues: each part has property P → the whole has property P. Choice C replicates this precisely: each chip operates at nanometer tolerances (part has P) → the processor operates at nanometer tolerances (whole has P). The property (operating precision) does not automatically transfer from part to whole — a processor's operational tolerance depends on integration, not merely component specs. Same compositional fallacy.
explanations.A: Superficially similar but the property shifts — 'drafted by a specialist' (process quality of parts) becomes 'masterwork' (evaluative quality of whole). The flaw here is more like an unsupported evaluative leap or equivocation, not a clean compositional fallacy. A trap for students who stop at 'parts → whole.'
explanations.B: This is the inverse — whole-to-part (division fallacy), not part-to-whole (composition fallacy). The argument infers a property of individual species from a property of the ecosystem. Different structural direction.
explanations.D: This is valid probabilistic reasoning. If most tiles are cobalt blue, the mosaic probably appears predominantly cobalt blue. The quantifier 'most' licenses the probabilistic conclusion. No flaw.
explanations.E: This is valid reasoning about aggregation of quantities: if each of N musicians rehearsed 100+ hours, the total hours rehearsed is necessarily large. Summing quantities across parts to get a total for the whole is logically sound — not a compositional fallacy.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal — the Carpaccio-tier flaw: most members of group X have property Y; this item has property Y; therefore it is probably an X. Answer choices use varied domains; one choice is a valid base-rate inference, one commits a different probabilistic error (ignoring a prior), and one is off-by-dimension (uses 'certainly' instead of 'probably'). Students must track both flaw type and conclusion strength.
stimulus: Most patients who contract the rare neurological disorder Valdenne's syndrome exhibit severe photosensitivity within the first month of onset. This patient has exhibited severe photosensitivity within the first month of her illness. Therefore, she probably has Valdenne's syndrome.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nearly all cases of acute mountain sickness involve a persistent headache. This climber has developed a persistent headache at altitude. Therefore, this climber probably has acute mountain sickness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most competitive long-distance runners follow a low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet. Tomás follows a low-fat, high-carbohydrate diet. Therefore, Tomás is certainly a competitive long-distance runner.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes report increased thirst and frequent urination. Dr. Fontaine has been diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes. Therefore, she probably experiences increased thirst and frequent urination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migratory birds account for the great majority of reported cases of avian influenza transmission to humans. This individual was recently infected with avian influenza. Therefore, the source of infection was probably a migratory bird.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A significant proportion of individuals who display early signs of cognitive decline are later diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Because early cognitive decline is increasingly common in adults over seventy, Alzheimer's disease is probably also increasingly common in that age group.

explanations.correct: The stimulus form: most X's have Y; this thing has Y; therefore it is probably an X. This reverses the base rate — having Y is common among X's, but that does not mean most Y-havers are X's (Y could be far more prevalent than X). Choice A replicates this exactly: nearly all cases of mountain sickness involve headache (most X's have Y); this climber has a headache (has Y); therefore probably has mountain sickness (probably an X). Headaches are extremely common and not specifically diagnostic of mountain sickness — the argument ignores the base rate of headaches generally.
explanations.A: Correct. Precise structural match: most X's have Y; item has Y; therefore item is probably X.
explanations.B: The flaw is the same type (base-rate reversal) but the conclusion says 'certainly' rather than 'probably.' The stimulus concludes 'probably,' so this is off-by-dimension on conclusion strength — a classic trap per the rubric.
explanations.C: This is valid reasoning. The argument moves from 'most X's have Y' and 'this individual is an X' to 'this individual probably has Y.' That is a straightforward base-rate application in the correct direction, not a reversal. No flaw.
explanations.D: Superficially similar — a conclusion about source drawn from a prevalence statistic — but the structure differs. The premise is about what accounts for most human cases (a different quantifier framing involving causal attribution), and the reasoning introduces a causal/source inference that the stimulus does not. A different flaw family.
explanations.E: This argument commits a different error: inferring that a trend in a risk factor (early cognitive decline increasing) causes a trend in the outcome (Alzheimer's increasing), without establishing whether the proportion who progress actually changes. This is closer to a base-rate/trend conflation or an unsupported causal inference — not the same structural move as the stimulus.
